items.relation_to_us: [domain] Incident-analysis LLM with source-file attribution but no verbatim quote check; telemetry input, not narratives.

items.title: Local LLM-Based Cyber Incident Analysis in Air-Gapped Networks via Teacher-Student Knowledge Distillation and Agentic Orchestration
items.authors: Sunghun Jang, MyoungRak Lee, Taeshik Shon
items.what_it_does: Distilled local model with a traceability matrix (EventID/time/PID anchors) and a learned factuality classifier; ablations on author-generated scenarios (full 88.4% vs no-agent 74.2%).
items.relation_to_us: [domain] Anchor checks plus learned verifier on telemetry; shows same-model verification ablations exist. Ours locates verbatim quotes in narrative sources.

items.title: An LLM-Based Agentic Network Traffic Incident-Report Approach Towards Explainable-AI Network Defense
items.authors: Chia-Hong Chou, Arjun Sudheer, Younghee Park
items.venue: Journal of Sensor and Actuator Networks 15(2):32, doi:10.3390/jsan15020032
items.what_it_does: Flow classifier plus SHAP plus ReAct tools write incident reports; faithfulness judged by an LLM of the same family (groundedness 1.0, faithfulness .6391 on 176/200 reports).
items.relation_to_us: [domain] Contrast: LLM-judged faithfulness and excluded failures vs our judge-free locator and counted failed cases.

items.title: Large Language Models Are Unreliable for Cyber Threat Intelligence
items.authors: E. Mezzi, F. Massacci, K. Tuma
items.what_it_does: Three LLMs on 350 CTI reports are inconsistent and overconfident; even small JSON outputs miss 10-28% of requested items; few-shot and fine-tuning did not help.
items.relation_to_us: [domain] Why CyberCase checks model output instead of trusting it, and why coverage (omission) is measured.

items.title: ChatGPT, Llama, can you write my report? An experiment on assisted digital forensics reports written using (local) large language models
items.authors: Gaetan Michelet, Frank Breitinger
items.venue: Forensic Science International: Digital Investigation 48, Art. 301683, doi:10.1016/j.fsidi.2023.301683
items.what_it_does: Derives the sections of a digital forensic report and tests ChatGPT and Llama on each; models can assist but output needs close checking.
items.relation_to_us: [domain] Supports keeping LLMs out of report writing; our report is a template over the stored analysis.

items.title: AGIR: Automating Cyber Threat Intelligence Reporting with Natural Language Generation
items.authors: Perrina, Marchiori, Conti, Verde
items.what_it_does: Templates turn STIX entities and relations into text, then ChatGPT rewrites for fluency.
items.relation_to_us: [domain] We keep the template stage and drop the LLM rewriter, after measuring that an LLM writer edits text it was told to copy.

items.title: Using Instruction-Tuned Large Language Models to Identify Indicators of Vulnerability in Police Incident Narratives
items.authors: Relins, Birks, Lloyd
items.venue: Journal of Quantitative Criminology 41(4), pp. 647-684, doi:10.1007/s10940-025-09611-z
items.what_it_does: Compares LLM and human coding of police incident narratives, measures label variability across repeated prompts, recommends human review of ambiguous cases.
items.relation_to_us: [domain] Crime-narrative LLM coding with human review; only the abstract was read (positioning audit), so cite for its stated aims only.

items.title: Extracting meaningful entities from police narrative reports
items.authors: Chau, Xu, Chen
items.what_it_does: Entities from police narratives by lexical lookup, machine learning and a few hand-written rules.
items.relation_to_us: [domain] Pre-LLM extraction is traceable by construction (fields are spans) but writes no summary, judgement or gaps; our locator restores span traceability for LLM-written claims.

items.title: Natural language processing and e-Government: crime information extraction from heterogeneous data sources
items.authors: Ku, Iriberri, Leroy
items.what_it_does: Extracts weapons, vehicles, time, people, clothes and locations from police reports and witness narratives; precision 96% / recall 83% on police narratives.
items.relation_to_us: [domain] Same contrast as Chau et al.: span extraction is traceable by construction but needs per-schema rules or labels.

items.title: Giveme5W1H: A Universal System for Extracting Main Events from News Articles
items.authors: Felix Hamborg, Corinna Breitinger, Bela Gipp
items.venue: INRA 2019 workshop (CEUR-WS 2554), arXiv 1909.02766; poster at JCDL 2018, doi:10.1145/3197026.3203899
items.what_it_does: Extracts a news article's main event as answers to who, what, when, where, why and how.
items.relation_to_us: [domain] CASIE is news and our gaps follow a 5W1H checklist; Giveme5W1H extracts what is present, our judgement records what is missing. Low priority for this paper.

items.title: Measuring Attribution in Natural Language Generation Models
items.authors: Hannah Rashkin, Vitaly Nikolaev, Matthew Lamm, Lora Aroyo, Michael Collins, Dipanjan Das, Slav Petrov, Gaurav Singh Tomar, Iulia Turc, David Reitter
items.evidence: ACL Anthology 2023.cl-4.2: "Measuring Attribution in Natural Language Generation Models" - Computational Linguistics, Volume 49, Issue 4, pages 777-840, 2023, DOI 10.1162/coli_a_00486.
items.supports: Attributable to Identified Sources (AIS) defines an output as attributable when a reader would judge it supported by a specific provided source; CyberCase's located quote is a necessary but not sufficient condition for AIS.
items.relation_to_us: Definitional frame. A 'verified' CyberCase quote only shows the span occurs in the cited case source; the AIS judgement (does the source support the claim) is the layer CyberCase does not automate. Cite AIS wherever the paper says 'grounded' or 'attributable'.
items.notes: CORRECTED author list: the candidate omitted the tenth author, David Reitter (listed last on the ACL Anthology page). The MIT Press landing page (direct.mit.edu) returned 403; metadata taken from the ACL Anthology page for the same DOI.

items.title: Teaching language models to support answers with verified quotes
items.authors: Jacob Menick, Maja Trebacz, Vladimir Mikulik, John Aslanides, Francis Song, Martin Chadwick, Mia Glaese, Susannah Young, Lucy Campbell-Gillingham, Geoffrey Irving, Nat McAleese
items.evidence: arXiv abs page: "Teaching language models to support answers with verified quotes", submitted 21 March 2022; no journal-ref or comments field.
items.supports: GopherCite (RLHP-trained) answers questions with verbatim quotes from retrieved documents and abstains when unsure, the canonical precedent for quote-backed answers.
items.relation_to_us: Contrast on the decoding axis: GopherCite guarantees exact quotes during decoding and relies on RL from human preferences; CyberCase's reading call has no grammar, checks quotes after decoding with a deterministic locator, does no training and no support judging. Cite as a preprint.
items.notes: Title and all 11 authors match the arXiv abs page. No peer-reviewed venue listed; a DBLP check was blocked (access denied), so 'preprint only' rests on the arXiv page carrying no journal-ref. The 80%/90% figures and the 'exact quotes' sentence come from the candidate's PDF reading and were not re-checked here.

items.title: Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations
items.authors: Tianyu Gao, Howard Yen, Jiatong Yu, Danqi Chen
items.evidence: ACL Anthology: "Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations" - Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, pages 6465-6488.
items.supports: ALCE evaluates LLM answers with inline passage citations using NLI-judged citation recall and citation precision.
items.relation_to_us: Reference point for citation evaluation. ALCE cites whole passages and judges entailment with a model; CyberCase cites verbatim spans and only checks that they occur in the source. Our traceable-claim rate is a weaker, mechanical analogue of citation recall; CyberCase has no precision or entailment metric.
items.notes: All fields match the ACL Anthology page.

items.title: Evaluating Verifiability in Generative Search Engines
items.authors: Nelson F. Liu, Tianyi Zhang, Percy Liang
items.evidence: ACL Anthology abstract: "on average, a mere 51.5% of generated sentences are fully supported by citations and only 74.5% of citations support their associated sentence." Findings of the ACL: EMNLP 2023, pp. 7001-7025.
items.supports: A human audit of four generative search engines found only 51.5% of generated sentences fully supported by their citations and 74.5% of citations supporting their sentence.
items.relation_to_us: Motivation for checking quotes rather than trusting them, and the source of the citation recall/precision vocabulary. CyberCase does not measure whether a citation supports its claim, which is what Liu et al. measure by hand; keep the 'verifiable, not verified-as-true' wording.
items.notes: The Anthology page lists the first author as 'Nelson Liu'; 'Nelson F. Liu' is the same author's usual form. DOI 10.18653/v1/2023.findings-emnlp.467.

items.title: Attribute First, then Generate: Locally-attributable Grounded Text Generation
items.authors: Aviv Slobodkin, Eran Hirsch, Arie Cattan, Tal Schuster, Ido Dagan
items.evidence: ACL Anthology: "Attribute First, then Generate: Locally-attributable Grounded Text Generation" - Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the ACL (Volume 1: Long Papers), pages 3309-3344.
items.supports: Separating content selection (choosing source spans) from generation ties each output sentence to short, pre-selected source spans.
items.relation_to_us: Design precedent for settling and checking the evidence before writing from it. CyberCase applies that order at claim level (reading -> quote check -> judgement over checked claims) but writes claims and quotes together, does not span-constrain the judgement, and renders the report from a template.
items.notes: All fields match the ACL Anthology page.

items.title: Learning Fine-Grained Grounded Citations for Attributed Large Language Models
items.authors: Lei Huang, Xiaocheng Feng, Weitao Ma, Yuxuan Gu, Weihong Zhong, Xiachong Feng, Weijiang Yu, Weihua Peng, Duyu Tang, Dandan Tu, Bing Qin
items.evidence: ACL Anthology abstract: "By initially grounding fine-grained supporting quotes, which then guide the generation process, these quotes not only provide supervision signals to improve citation quality but also serve as fine-grained attributions."
items.supports: FRONT trains an LLM to ground fine-grained supporting quotes first and then generate conditioned on them, improving ALCE citation quality by an average of 14.21% with LLaMA-2-7B.
items.relation_to_us: Shows that 'quotes before conclusions' is an established pattern, not CyberCase's novelty. FRONT does it inside one trained model and evaluates with NLI-based support; CyberCase uses two prompted calls with a deterministic quote check between them, no training and no support metric.
items.notes: All fields match the ACL Anthology page; DOI 10.18653/v1/2024.findings-acl.838. The 14.21% figure is from the abstract on that page.

items.title: LongCite: Enabling LLMs to Generate Fine-grained Citations in Long-Context QA
items.authors: Jiajie Zhang, Yushi Bai, Xin Lv, Wanjun Gu, Danqing Liu, Minhao Zou, Shulin Cao, Lei Hou, Yuxiao Dong, Ling Feng, Juanzi Li
items.evidence: ACL Anthology abstract: responses "with fine-grained sentence-level citations on the fly, thereby improving their faithfulness and verifiability." Findings of the ACL: ACL 2025, pp. 5098-5122.
items.supports: LongCite trains long-context LLMs to cite sentence-indexed spans of the context and evaluates citation recall and precision on LongBench-Cite.
items.relation_to_us: Design trade-off: index-based citations cannot mis-quote but cite whole sentences; CyberCase's free-text verbatim quotes can point to sub-sentence spans but can fail to locate, which is why it needs the tiered locator and near-match pointer. LongCite also uses an LLM judge for support, which CyberCase does not.
items.notes: All fields match the ACL Anthology page; DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.findings-acl.264. Details on the GPT-4o judge, the LongCite-45k set and the [6-8] index format come from the candidate, not from the landing page.

items.title: Verifiable by Construction: Claim-Level Evaluation of Verbatim Citation in Clinical Question Answering
items.authors: Jiashuo Zhang, Yuling Chen, Yvonne Commodore-Mensah, Michael Oberst
items.evidence: arXiv abstract: "claude-opus-5 produces verbatim quotes for 98.0% of its claims, but fully substantiates only 37.1%."
items.supports: In clinical QA, a model attached verbatim quotes to 98.0% of its claims but fully substantiated only 37.1%, so a quote that is verbatim does not make the claim supported.
items.relation_to_us: Closest evaluation design: their 'is the quote verbatim' stage is what CyberCase's locator does, and their substantiation stage is exactly the layer we do not check. Cite as a preprint and as the reason for the 'verifiable, not verified-as-true' wording.
items.notes: Submitted 14 Sep 2026 (v1), revised 17 Sep 2026 (v2); no journal-ref or comments. The candidate's '98.0%' is credited on the page to a specific model (claude-opus-5); say so when citing.

items.title: DeepFaith: Evidence-Grounded LLMs for Faithful Incident Reporting in Multi-Stage APT Defense
items.authors: Trung V. Phan, Tri Gia Nguyen, Thomas Bauschert
items.venue: arXiv:2607.24348 (preprint; comments: submitted to IEEE CNSM 2026)
items.evidence: arXiv abstract: "DeepFaith improves faithfulness from 0.68 to 0.92, reduces unsupported claims from 0.32 to 0.08, and increases temporal consistency from 0.6 to 0.88". Comments: submitted to IEEE CNSM 2026.
items.supports: DeepFaith generates incident reports for APT defense from structured telemetry with evidence-grounded prompting and post-generation verification, raising faithfulness from 0.68 to 0.92.
items.relation_to_us: Closest system with the same goal (faithful, evidence-grounded incident reports), but its input is machine telemetry and an LLM writes the report with a reject-and-regenerate verifier; there is no verbatim-quote protocol. Its template baseline means template rendering is not CyberCase's novelty.
items.notes: The arXiv comments field says 'submitted to' CNSM 2026, not accepted; treat as an unreviewed preprint. Submitted 27 July 2026.

items.title: Retrieval-Augmented LLMs for Security Incident Analysis
items.authors: Xavier Cadet, Aditya Vikram Singh, Harsh Mamania, Edward Koh, Alex Fitts, Dirk Van Bruggen, Simona Boboila, Peter Chin, Alina Oprea
items.venue: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems (CAIS '26), San Jose, CA, pp. 103-123 (peer-reviewed); also arXiv:2603.18196
items.evidence: Crossref for DOI 10.1145/3786335.3813136: container-title "Proceedings of the ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems", event "CAIS '26: ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems", San Jose CA USA, pages 103-123, published 2026-05-26.
items.supports: A RAG system over security logs answers analyst questions and assembles an incident report, reaching 94% average indicator recall (Claude Sonnet 4) across 17 malware scenarios.
items.relation_to_us: Closest peer-reviewed incident-analysis system that cites its sources, but at chunk or file level over logs, with no check that quoted text occurs in a source and no entailment check. Places CyberCase as narrative-source, span-level traceability against log-based, chunk-level citation.
items.notes: CORRECTED venue: CAIS is the 'ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems', not the 'Conference on Artificial Intelligence for Cybersecurity' as the candidate said. The ACM DL page returned 403; venue and pages taken from the Crossref record for the DOI and confirmed by the arXiv comments field ('In ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems, CAIS 2026, San Jose, CA, USA'). Neither landing page shows the '129 questions' figure; check it in the full text before citing it.

themes.theme: Checking whether a source supports generated text (factual consistency / faithfulness / attribution checkers), and evidence that a verbatim quote can be present in the source and still not support the claim

items.title: Verifiable by Construction: Claim-Level Evaluation of Verbatim Citation in Clinical Question Answering
items.authors: Jiashuo Zhang, Yuling Chen, Yvonne Commodore-Mensah, Michael Oberst
items.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.15964 (cs.CL; v1 14 Sep 2026, v2 17 Sep 2026); no journal-ref
items.evidence: "claude-opus-5 produces verbatim quotes for 98.0% of its claims, but fully substantiates only 37.1%." (arXiv abs page, abstract)
items.supports: A quote that is present verbatim in the source can still fail to substantiate the claim: in clinical QA the best model quoted verbatim for 98.0% of claims but fully substantiated only 37.1%.
items.relation_to_us: Closest precedent for our locator. Its exact, normalized and elided tiers nearly match ours, so the locator tiers cannot be claimed as new. It is also the most direct evidence for the theme, and the reason we call a located quote 'verified' (verifiable) and not 'supported'. It adds an LLM substantiation judge, which we do not have. Their domain is clinical QA over guidelines; ours is cybercrime case narratives, with a near-match pointer for quotes that cannot be located.
items.notes: The arXiv abs page confirms title, all four authors, v1 (14 Sep 2026) and v2 (17 Sep 2026), and cs.CL. It lists no journal-ref, so cite it as a preprint. The three-stage ladder and the tier details (12 LLMs, 222 questions, four guidelines) come from the repo's full-text reading notes; I did not re-check them on the landing page.

items.title: Extractive is not Faithful: An Investigation of Broad Unfaithfulness Problems in Extractive Summarization
items.authors: Shiyue Zhang, David Wan, Mohit Bansal
items.venue: Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), pp. 2153-2174, doi:10.18653/v1/2023.acl-long.120
items.evidence: "30% of the summaries have at least one of the five issues" (ACL Anthology abstract); five problems: "incorrect coreference, incomplete coreference, incorrect discourse, incomplete discourse, as well as other misleading information"
items.supports: Text copied verbatim from a source can still be unfaithful: 30% of 1,600 extractive summaries from 16 systems had at least one coreference, discourse or misleading-context problem.
items.relation_to_us: Peer-reviewed evidence that verbatim does not mean faithful. A quote lifted out of its context, for example with an unresolved pronoun or missing discourse, can mislead, and our located quotes carry the same risk. The stored sentence around each quote (trace/sentences.py; supporting_contexts in the report) helps a human reader with coreference and discourse, but it is not a check, and the paper should say so.
items.notes: Every field matches the landing page. The abstract confirms 1,600 summaries, 16 systems and the ExtEval metric.

items.title: SummaC: Re-Visiting NLI-based Models for Inconsistency Detection in Summarization
items.authors: Philippe Laban, Tobias Schnabel, Paul N. Bennett, Marti A. Hearst
items.venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, vol. 10, pp. 163-177, doi:10.1162/tacl_a_00453
items.evidence: "enables NLI models to be successfully used for this task by segmenting documents into sentence units and aggregating scores between pairs of sentences" (ACL Anthology abstract)
items.supports: NLI models detect summary inconsistency with the source well when applied at sentence granularity, which makes sentence-level entailment a standard way to check source support.
items.relation_to_us: Same goal (does the source support the generated text), different method: learned entailment where we use deterministic string location. It is the standard NLI layer we do not run. A located quote plus its stored sentence context could serve as the premise if such a layer were added. Thai sources would need a multilingual NLI model. This is unmeasured: state it as a limitation, not a result.
items.notes: Every field matches the landing page. In the abstract, the sentence-segmentation wording describes SummaCConv specifically.

items.title: MiniCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of LLMs on Grounding Documents
items.authors: Liyan Tang, Philippe Laban, Greg Durrett
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), pp. 8818-8847, doi:10.18653/v1/2024.emnlp-main.499
items.evidence: "We show how to build small fact-checking models that have GPT-4-level performance but for 400x lower cost." (ACL Anthology abstract)
items.supports: Small trained checkers can judge whether a grounding document supports an LLM-generated sentence, with GPT-4-level accuracy at 400x lower cost.
items.relation_to_us: Current practical state of the art for the layer we leave out: whether a grounding document supports an LLM sentence. It is the most realistic candidate if the paper discusses adding a support check after the locator. Our locator answers a narrower, deterministic question (is this exact text in the source), so the two are complementary, not competing.
items.notes: Every field matches the landing page. The LLM-AggreFact benchmark is described in the abstract; I did not quote it separately.

items.title: AlignScore: Evaluating Factual Consistency with A Unified Alignment Function
items.authors: Yuheng Zha, Yichi Yang, Ruichen Li, Zhiting Hu
items.venue: Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), pp. 11328-11348, doi:10.18653/v1/2023.acl-long.634
items.evidence: "a general function of information alignment between two arbitrary text pieces"; "4.7M training examples from 7 well-established tasks" (ACL Anthology abstract)
items.supports: Factual consistency between a source and generated text can be scored by one learned alignment function, trained on 4.7M examples from seven tasks.
items.relation_to_us: Same goal, different method: a learned continuous alignment score where we use string location. Contrast: our near-match pointer deliberately shows no similarity score and leaves the judgement to a person. Cite it as one of the support checkers whose layer we do not implement.
items.notes: Every field matches the landing page. The seven tasks named in the abstract are NLI, QA, paraphrasing, fact verification, information retrieval, semantic similarity and summarization.

items.title: Evaluating the Factual Consistency of Abstractive Text Summarization
items.authors: Wojciech Kryscinski, Bryan McCann, Caiming Xiong, Richard Socher
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), pp. 9332-9346, doi:10.18653/v1/2020.emnlp-main.750
items.evidence: "We propose a weakly-supervised, model-based approach for verifying factual consistency and identifying conflicts between source documents and generated summaries." (ACL Anthology abstract)
items.supports: FactCC verifies factual consistency between a source document and a generated summary with a weakly supervised model; one variant also extracts the source span behind its prediction and the inconsistent span in the summary.
items.relation_to_us: An early learned support checker (same goal, different method). Its span-extraction variant is a loose precedent for our near-match pointer, which points the reader at a source passage and the words that differ. Ours does this only for quotes that cannot be located, and makes no consistency prediction.
items.notes: Every field matches the landing page. Span extraction is confirmed in the abstract: "Extract a span in the source document to support this consistency prediction". The rule-based training transformations come from the candidate description; I did not quote them separately.

items.title: Asking and Answering Questions to Evaluate the Factual Consistency of Summaries
items.authors: Alex Wang, Kyunghyun Cho, Mike Lewis
items.venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, pp. 5008-5020, doi:10.18653/v1/2020.acl-main.450
items.evidence: "Existing automatic evaluation metrics for summarization are largely insensitive to such errors." (ACL Anthology abstract)
items.supports: QAGS checks whether a summary is consistent with its source by asking questions of both and comparing the answers, a question-answering alternative to entailment-based checking.
items.relation_to_us: The QA-based family of support checkers, a second method family beside NLI. Same goal, a layer we do not implement. Cite it with SummaC, AlignScore and MiniCheck in one sentence saying that semantic support checking exists and is outside our scope.
items.notes: Every field matches the landing page.

items.title: TRUE: Re-evaluating Factual Consistency Evaluation
items.authors: Or Honovich, Roee Aharoni, Jonathan Herzig, Hagai Taitelbaum, Doron Kukliansy, Vered Cohen, Thomas Scialom, Idan Szpektor, Avinatan Hassidim, Yossi Matias
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2022 Conference of the North American Chapter of the ACL: Human Language Technologies (NAACL-HLT 2022), pp. 3905-3920, doi:10.18653/v1/2022.naacl-main.287
items.evidence: "large-scale NLI and question generation-and-answering-based approaches achieve strong and complementary results" (ACL Anthology abstract)
items.supports: A meta-evaluation over 11 standardized datasets found that large NLI checkers and question-generation-and-answering checkers give strong and complementary results for factual consistency.
items.relation_to_us: The meta-evaluation behind the NLI checkers we cite. ALCE, already in the repo, uses a TRUE-trained NLI model for its citation recall and precision, so TRUE links our string-level 'verified' to the entailment-level citation metrics we explicitly do not compute.
items.notes: Every field matches the landing page, including all ten authors in order and the 11 datasets. I did not re-check the ALCE link on ALCE's own page here.

items.title: Measuring Attribution in Natural Language Generation Models
items.authors: Hannah Rashkin, Vitaly Nikolaev, Matthew Lamm, Lora Aroyo, Michael Collins, Dipanjan Das, Slav Petrov, Gaurav Singh Tomar, Iulia Turc, David Reitter
items.venue: Computational Linguistics, vol. 49, no. 4, pp. 777-840, doi:10.1162/coli_a_00486
items.evidence: "NLG output pertaining to the external world is to be verified against an independent, provided source." (ACL Anthology abstract, AIS definition)
items.supports: Attributable to Identified Sources (AIS) defines when generated output counts as supported by a provided source and gives a human annotation protocol for judging it.
items.relation_to_us: The definition our 'verified' status must be contrasted with. A located quote shows that the cited text exists in the source, not that the claim is AIS-attributable. The paper should name AIS as the judgement our pipeline leaves to the human reader.
items.notes: Confirmed on the landing page: 10 authors, ending with David Reitter. The repo table at docs/thesis/related_studies_modules.md line 260 lists only 9 authors and omits Reitter, so fix that row; references.bib key 'ais' is correct.

items.title: Automatic Evaluation of Attribution by Large Language Models
items.authors: Xiang Yue, Boshi Wang, Ziru Chen, Kai Zhang, Yu Su, Huan Sun
items.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2023, pp. 4615-4635, doi:10.18653/v1/2023.findings-emnlp.307
items.evidence: "verifying whether the generated statement is fully supported by the cited reference" (ACL Anthology abstract); test set covers "12 domains from a generative search engine, New Bing"
items.supports: AttrScore uses prompted or fine-tuned LMs to judge whether a cited reference fully supports a generated statement, and separates references that support the claim, lack the information to validate it, or contradict it.
items.relation_to_us: Its 'extrapolatory' category (the reference lacks sufficient information to validate the claim) names exactly the case our locator cannot detect: the cited text exists but does not carry the claim. An LLM attribution judge is a layer we do not implement; we report traceability (quote located) and leave support to a person.
items.notes: Bibliographic fields match the ACL Anthology page (the arXiv 2305.06311 journal-ref also says EMNLP 2023 Findings). The abstract only says "different types of attribution errors" and does not name the three categories. The names attributable, extrapolatory and contradictory come from the authors' GitHub README (OSU-NLP-Group/AttrScore), where extrapolatory is "the reference lacks sufficient information to validate the claim". The candidate quoted "...validate the generated answer", which I could not confirm on any landing page; quote the README wording or check the paper body before quoting.

items.title: The theory and computation of evolutionary distances: Pattern recognition
items.authors: Peter H. Sellers
items.evidence: Crossref record for the DOI: title 'The theory and computation of evolutionary distances: Pattern recognition', author Peter H Sellers, container 'Journal of Algorithms', vol 1, issue 4, pages 359-373, 1980-12.
items.supports: The near-match pointer computes the semi-global (infix) edit distance introduced by Sellers (1980), in which a match may begin and end anywhere in the source.
items.relation_to_us: Direct precedent for one component. infix_alignment in backend/app/trace/quotes.py is this recurrence: previous=[0]*(width+1), the end is the minimum of the last row, and a traceback gives the differing words. Cite it as the origin of the near-match pointer's distance and claim no novelty for it.
items.notes: The elsevier landing page redirect was not readable; metadata taken from the Crossref record of the DOI. The Navarro (2001) credit sentence was confirmed in Navarro's own copy of the survey (see the Navarro item).

items.title: Identification of common molecular subsequences
items.authors: Temple F. Smith, Michael S. Waterman
items.evidence: Crossref record for the DOI: title 'Identification of common molecular subsequences', authors T.F. Smith, M.S. Waterman, 'Journal of Molecular Biology', vol 147, issue 1, pages 195-197, 1981-03.
items.supports: Local alignment (Smith and Waterman, 1981) may align only part of a quote, so the pointer instead uses infix alignment, which forces the whole quote onto one source passage.
items.relation_to_us: A neighbouring method that we chose not to use. Local alignment may align only part of a quote. Our infix alignment forces the whole quote onto one source passage, so a quote that matches only partly cannot look like a full match. Cite it to explain why the pointer is semi-global rather than local.
items.notes: Metadata from Crossref (publisher page redirect not readable). The candidate's mention of Wilkerson et al. 2015 AJPS was not checked here. The Passim JCDL 2014 paper does use the Smith-Waterman algorithm (verified in its PDF: 'Even the exact Smith-Waterman algorithm, however, is an approximation to the problem we aim to solve').

items.title: A guided tour to approximate string matching
items.authors: Gonzalo Navarro
items.evidence: Crossref: 'A guided tour to approximate string matching', Navarro, Gonzalo, ACM Computing Surveys 33(1):31-88, 2001. Survey text: 'it was converted into a search algorithm only in 1980 by Sellers'.
items.supports: The pointer follows the filter-then-verify pattern surveyed by Navarro (2001): a cheap filter proposes a window and an exact dynamic program verifies inside it.
items.relation_to_us: Background citation. The near-match pointer is a filter-then-verify scheme of the kind this survey describes: rapidfuzz partial_ratio_alignment proposes a window, and an exact infix dynamic program runs inside the window, padded by the quote length on each side. Cite it once for the general technique rather than citing each algorithm.
items.notes: Metadata from Crossref. The Sellers sentence and the filtering description ('algorithms that filter the text, quickly discarding text areas which cannot match') were read in the author's copy at users.dcc.uchile.cl/~gnavarro/ps/acmcs01.1.pdf; digits were lost in PDF extraction there, so cite the published version for page-exact quotes.

items.title: Edlib: a C/C++ library for fast, exact sequence alignment using edit distance
items.authors: Martin Šošić, Mile Šikić
items.evidence: PubMed 28453688: 'Bioinformatics. 2017 May 1;33(9):1394-1395. Edlib: a C/C ++ library for fast, exact sequence alignment using edit distance.' Full text: 'gaps at the start and at the end of the query sequence are not penalized (infix method)'.
items.supports: Edlib (Šošić and Šikić, 2017) computes the same infix edit-distance alignment and path with Myers's bit-vector algorithm and could replace the pure-Python dynamic program if speed on long sources mattered.
items.relation_to_us: Precedent for a component, and an engineering option. It computes the same infix alignment and path that our pure-Python O(mn) infix_alignment computes, only faster. The output, including the path for the differing words, would be the same, so it could replace that function if speed on long sources ever matters.
items.notes: Correction: the paper (PMC5408825) defines the infix method as the semi-global method where gaps at the start and end of the QUERY sequence are not penalized, not the 'target' as the candidate said. Author names carry diacritics (Šošić, Šikić). Metadata from Crossref and PubMed; OUP page redirect not read.

items.title: Detecting and modeling local text reuse
items.authors: David A. Smith, Ryan Cordell, Elizabeth Maddock Dillon, Nick Stramp, John Wilkerson
items.venue: IEEE/ACM Joint Conference on Digital Libraries (JCDL 2014), pp. 183-192
items.evidence: Abstract (author PDF): 'We describe and evaluate efficient algorithms for detecting clusters of reused passages embedded within longer documents in large collections.'
items.supports: Text-reuse systems such as Passim (Smith et al., 2014) also pair cheap n-gram candidates with alignment, but they discover unknown reuse across a corpus, whereas we check one quote against its cited source.
items.relation_to_us: Same two-stage shape (cheap candidates, then alignment), used for a different task. Passim discovers unknown reuse across a corpus and tolerates OCR noise as reuse. We are given one quote and its cited source and decide only whether it is there. Any difference in letters or digits leaves the quote unlocated, and the difference is shown to a person through the pointer, never counted as a match.
items.notes: Crossref has venue 2014 IEEE/ACM JCDL, pages 183-192, 2014-09, but misspells 'Cordel'; the PDF (ccs.neu.edu/home/dasmith/infect-dl-2014.pdf) gives Ryan Cordell. The PDF confirms 'overlapping n-grams to prune dynamic programming for local alignment' and 'noisy OCR' 19c newspapers plus Congressional bills. The name 'Passim' is not in this abstract; Vesanto et al. (2017) refer to it as 'Passim (Smith et al., 2014)'. The earlier paper is also verified via Crossref: Smith, Cordell, Dillon, 'Infectious texts: Modeling text reuse in nineteenth-century newspapers', 2013 IEEE International Conference on Big Data, pp. 86-94, doi:10.1109/BigData.2013.6691675.

items.title: A System for Identifying and Exploring Text Repetition in Large Historical Document Corpora
items.authors: Aleksi Vesanto, Asko Nivala, Tapio Salakoski, Hannu Salmi, Filip Ginter
items.venue: Proceedings of the 21st Nordic Conference on Computational Linguistics (NoDaLiDa 2017), pp. 330-333, Gothenburg
items.evidence: PDF: 'The system combines NCBI BLAST, a software created for comparing and aligning biological sequences, with the Solr search and indexing engine'; corpus of 'Finnish newspapers and journals from years 1771 to 1910'.
items.supports: Historical text-reuse systems tolerate OCR noise with an aligner and leave the judgement to a person browsing the aligned passages (Vesanto et al., 2017), the role our near-match pointer plays.
items.relation_to_us: Precedent for tolerating OCR noise with an alignment tool and leaving the judgement to a human reading the aligned passages, which is the role of our near-match pointer. Our sources can also be OCR output (Typhoon OCR), but our locator never accepts noise as verification: noisy matches go to the pointer only.
items.notes: Author order differs between sources: the PDF lists Vesanto, Nivala, Salakoski, Salmi, Ginter (used here, matches the candidate); the ACL Anthology page metadata lists Vesanto, Ginter, Salmi, Nivala, Salakoski. The Anthology treats the PDF as authoritative. The PDF header reads 'Nordic Conference of Computational Linguistics'; the Anthology volume reads 'on'. The PDF also says Passim relies on seed overlaps several full words long, which their OCR (25-30% word error) rarely provides.

items.title: Teaching language models to support answers with verified quotes
items.authors: Jacob Menick, Maja Trebacz, Vladimir Mikulik, John Aslanides, Francis Song, Martin Chadwick, Mia Glaese, Susannah Young, Lucy Campbell-Gillingham, Geoffrey Irving, Nat McAleese
items.evidence: Paper text: 'Constrained sampling ensures that the model quotes are verbatim from the claimed source.'
items.supports: GopherCite (Menick et al., 2022) enforces verbatim quotes during decoding with constrained sampling, whereas our reading call decodes without a grammar and checks its quotes afterwards.
items.relation_to_us: Same goal (a verbatim quote as checkable evidence for a claim), different method. They force verbatim quotes during decoding. Our reading call has no grammar, and its quotes are checked afterwards, which is the decoding factor in our 2x2. Their ROUGE-L evidence baseline is the 'repair by nearest passage' route that we deliberately do not take.
items.notes: arXiv API: v1 only (2022-03-21), no journal_ref, no DOI. PDF also confirms: after SFT the model 'produces perfect verbatim quotes on held out data around 75% of the time, even without constrained sampling', and the ROUGE-L 'closest-matching sequence of n+2 sentences' evidence baseline (used for ELI5).

items.title: "According to ...": Prompting Language Models Improves Quoting from Pre-Training Data
items.authors: Orion Weller, Marc Marone, Nathaniel Weir, Dawn Lawrie, Daniel Khashabi, Benjamin Van Durme
items.venue: Proceedings of the 18th Conference of the European Chapter of the ACL (EACL 2024), Volume 1: Long Papers, pp. 2288-2301, St. Julian's, Malta
items.evidence: Abstract: 'we propose a novel evaluation metric (QUIP-Score) that measures the extent to which model-produced answers are directly found in underlying text corpora.'
items.supports: QUIP-Score (Weller et al., 2024) also measures quoting deterministically by string membership, but over n-grams anywhere in a corpus rather than a whole quote in the one source it cites.
items.relation_to_us: A deterministic string-based measure of quoting, like our traceable claim rate, but it measures something else. QUIP is a fraction of n-grams found anywhere in a pretraining corpus, with possible Bloom-filter false positives. We locate the whole quote in the specific source it cites.
items.notes: ACL Anthology BibTeX confirms authors, booktitle, pages 2288-2301, doi 10.18653/v1/2024.eacl-long.140. The Data Portraits Bloom-filter detail comes from the repo reading notes and was not re-read here.

items.title: Verifiable by Construction: Claim-Level Evaluation of Verbatim Citation in Clinical Question Answering
items.authors: Jiashuo Zhang, Yuling Chen, Yvonne Commodore-Mensah, Michael Oberst
items.evidence: Abstract: 'claude-opus-5 produces verbatim quotes for 98.0% of its claims, but fully substantiates only 37.1%.'
items.supports: A quote that is verbatim need not support its claim (Zhang et al., 2026), so we call a located quote verifiable rather than verified as true.
items.relation_to_us: The closest precedent for our locator tiers (NFKC, ellipsis pieces, markup-tolerant, format-only). Same goal, almost the same method, so the tiers cannot be presented as new. Their support result backs our wording that a located quote is 'verifiable', not 'verified as true'. Their LLM support judge is a layer we do not build.
items.notes: Corrections: the metric is the 'Verbatim Compliance Rate (VCR)', not 'Verbatim Citation Rate'. For claude-opus-5 the coverage table shows VCR 100.0, with 98.0% of claims covered by a verbatim quote and 37.1% fully supported. The judge (deepseek-v4-flash) was validated, not calibrated, against two human annotators on a stratified sample of 70 cases (kappa 0.858 and 0.810). Elided tier: fragments shorter than ten characters are disregarded and at least two must remain. arXiv v2 (2026-09-17), no journal_ref.

items.title: Show Your Work: Verbatim Evidence Requirements and Automated Assessment of Large Language Models for Biomedical Text Processing of Trial Eligibility Criteria
items.authors: Paul Windisch, Julia Weyrich, Fabio Dennstädt, Daniel R. Zwahlen, Robert Förster, Christina Schröder
items.evidence: Full text (PMC13252682): 'A quote was considered mechanically valid only if the normalized quote appeared as an exact, contiguous substring of the normalized abstract.'
items.supports: Strict substring checks after whitespace normalization (Windisch et al., 2026) are the baseline our locator relaxes only for formatting differences.
items.relation_to_us: The strict baseline: their check is roughly our exact tier. Our later tiers relax only formatting (NFKC, markup, quote marks, punctuation, dash style, case). Their LLM support judge is a layer we do not use, and the repo notes say no metric of ours may copy that design.
items.notes: PubMed 42281695 confirms Cureus 2026 May 11;18(5):e108666. Author names carry diacritics (Dennstädt, Förster, Schröder). Abstract confirms mechanically valid quotes in 83.3% to 91.2% of runs and 48.0% to 78.8% judged semantically supported. Normalization: whitespace runs collapsed, leading and trailing quotation marks stripped.

items.title: OpenNovelty: An LLM-powered Agentic System for Verifiable Scholarly Novelty Assessment
items.authors: Ming Zhang, Kexin Tan, Yueyuan Huang, Yujiong Shen, Chunchun Ma, Li Ju, Xinran Zhang, Yuhui Wang, Wenqing Jing, Jingyi Deng, Huayu Sha, Binze Hu, Jingqi Tong, Changhao Jiang, Yage Geng, Yuankai Ying, Yue Zhang, Zhangyue Yin, Zhiheng Xi, Shihan Dou, Tao Gui, Qi Zhang, Xuanjing Huang
items.evidence: Paper text: 'A quote is considered verified if its confidence score exceeds 0.6, computed as a weighted combination of anchor coverage and hit ratio'.
items.supports: OpenNovelty (Zhang et al., 2026) also downgrades a judgement that lacks verified quotes, but it accepts fuzzy matches above a 0.6 score as verified, whereas we accept only exact letter-and-digit matches and leave near matches to a person.
items.relation_to_us: The same policy shape as ours: a claim without a verified quote is downgraded, just as our 'reported' becomes 'not_confirmed'. The difference is that they accept a fuzzy score above a threshold as 'verified'. We accept only quotes whose letters and digits match exactly, and we show near matches without a score for a person to judge. This is a useful contrast for explaining why no similarity score is shown.
items.notes: arXiv v2 (2026-01-19), no journal_ref. HTML full text confirms difflib SequenceMatcher over lowercased tokens with leading and trailing punctuation removed, and that 'any can_refute judgment lacking verified evidence is automatically downgraded to cannot_refute'.

items.title: Verifying LLM-extracted text with token alignment (v1 title: Token Alignment for Verifying LLM-Extracted Text)
items.authors: A. Sina Booeshaghi, Aaron M. Streets
items.evidence: Abstract: 'A simple way to avoid hallucinations is to remove any extracted text that does not appear in the original source.'
items.supports: Ordered token alignment of discontiguous extractions (Booeshaghi and Streets, 2026) generalises our ellipsis-pieces tier, which accepts pieces only when an ellipsis marks them and each occurs once.
items.relation_to_us: Same goal: keep only quoted text that is in the source. Their ordered alignment of discontiguous text is a general version of our ellipsis-pieces tier, which accepts pieces only when an ellipsis marks them and each piece occurs once. BOAT could serve as an outside test set for the locator.
items.notes: bioRxiv API: both versions have published = 'NA' (no journal version). Abstract confirms subword ordered alignment improves alignment 'by about 50% compared to word-level tokenization', the BOAT dataset (SQuAD with non-contiguous phrases), BIO-BOAT from 51 bioRxiv preprints, and the tool taln. Crossref lists the second author as 'Aaron Streets'; bioRxiv lists 'Streets, A. M.'.

themes.theme: Structured output from LLMs: grammar-constrained decoding versus prompting plus validation; effect of format restrictions on quality; validate-and-retry libraries; failure modes such as whitespace runaway under grammars

items.title: Let Me Speak Freely? A Study on the Impact of Format Restrictions on Large Language Model Performance
items.authors: Zhi Rui Tam, Cheng-Kuang Wu, Yi-Lin Tsai, Chieh-Yen Lin, Hung-yi Lee, Yun-Nung Chen
items.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: Industry Track, pp. 1218-1236 (November 2024)
items.evidence: ACL Anthology: "Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: Industry Track", pages 1218-1236. arXiv abstract: "we find that stricter format constraints generally lead to greater performance degradation in reasoning tasks."
items.supports: Format restrictions on LLM output, from format-restricting instructions to JSON-mode decoding, can lower accuracy on reasoning tasks, and stricter restrictions tend to hurt more.
items.relation_to_us: The same question as the decoding axis of our 2x2, measured on short-answer benchmarks. Our reading call is their format-restricting-instructions condition plus validation after decoding and up to two re-asks; our judgement call is their JSON-mode condition. Our outcomes are traceable-claim rate and citation coverage on long extraction outputs with verbatim quotations, not reasoning accuracy. Cite it as the canonical 'format restrictions change quality' result and note that the literature disagrees (JSONSchemaBench; the .txt 'Say What You Mean' rebuttal, grey literature).
items.notes: Title, authors, venue and pages match the Anthology page. The arXiv version (2408.02442) carries a slightly different title ('...on Performance of Large Language Models'); cite the Anthology title. The per-condition details (JSON-mode worst on reasoning, JSON-mode helping classification) come from repo notes and were not rechecked here; the abstract confirms only the reasoning decline and the stricter-is-worse trend.

items.title: JSONSchemaBench: A Rigorous Benchmark of Structured Outputs for Language Models
items.authors: Saibo Geng, Hudson Cooper, Michał Moskal, Samuel Jenkins, Julian Berman, Nathan Ranchin, Robert West, Eric Horvitz, Harsha Nori
items.venue: arXiv 2501.10868 (preprint; v1 18 Jan 2025, v3 27 Feb 2025; no Comments or Journal-ref on the abs page). The first author's CV lists it as 'ICML 2025 ES-FoMo III Workshop' (non-archival workshop)
items.evidence: arXiv abs title: "JSONSchemaBench: A Rigorous Benchmark of Structured Outputs for Language Models"; first author's CV: "arxiv.org/abs/2501.10868 (ICML 2025 ES-FoMo III Workshop)".
items.supports: A benchmark of about 10K real-world JSON schemas shows that constrained-decoding frameworks differ widely in efficiency and schema coverage, and on three short reasoning tasks the constrained frameworks scored slightly above unconstrained generation.
items.relation_to_us: The framework-side benchmark, and its quality result points the other way from Tam et al. It assumes the client controls the engine and short outputs; it does not diagnose whitespace runaway or measure multi-thousand-token outputs. We work on the application side, behind a router (OpenRouter), and cannot choose the engine. Our 2x2 adds a long-output, quotation-bearing data point to this disagreement.
items.notes: Correction to the candidate: the 'about 3 points' gain is Guidance's ("approximately a 3% improvement over the LM-only approach in every task", Table 8); XGrammar gained 0.1-3.6 points and Outlines 0.4-2.6. The quality experiment uses one model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) and the prompts and schemas from the .txt rebuttal. The GitHub BibTeX still uses the v1 title 'Generating Structured Outputs from Language Models: Benchmark and Studies'. DBLP was blocked by a bot check and was not read. Cite as an arXiv preprint (optionally adding the workshop); do not cite it as an ICML main-conference paper.

items.title: XGrammar: Flexible and Efficient Structured Generation Engine for Large Language Models
items.authors: Yixin Dong, Charlie F. Ruan, Yaxing Cai, Ziyi Xu, Yilong Zhao, Ruihang Lai, Tianqi Chen
items.venue: Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems 7 (MLSys 2025); arXiv 2411.15100
items.evidence: MLSys page: "Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems 7 (MLSys 2025) Conference"; abstract: "XGrammar can more than 10x faster than existing solutions for structure generation."
items.supports: XGrammar is a widely deployed context-free-grammar engine for constrained decoding that splits the vocabulary into context-independent and context-dependent tokens to make grammar checking nearly free at serving time.
items.relation_to_us: Probably the engine behind the hosted providers that served our grammar-constrained calls; this is inferred from the symptom, since the providers do not say which engine they run. Its JSON-schema compiler allows unbounded whitespace unless max_whitespace_cnt is set (default None per the XGrammar API docs and the vLLM/oMLX issues). That is the layer we cannot reach through a router, which is why the reading call drops the grammar instead of changing the engine.
items.notes: Author order differs between sources: the MLSys proceedings list Ruihang Lai sixth (as in the candidate), arXiv lists him fourth; use the proceedings order when citing MLSys. The MLSys abstract says 'more than 10x'; the arXiv abstract says 'up to 100x speedup'. The max_whitespace_cnt default is from XGrammar docs and GitHub issues found by search, not from the paper; the claim that it is the default backend in vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and MLC-LLM was not rechecked here.

items.title: Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models
items.authors: Brandon T. Willard, Rémi Louf
items.venue: arXiv 2307.09702 (preprint; v1 19 Jul 2023, v4 19 Aug 2023; no Comments or Journal-ref on the abs page)
items.evidence: arXiv abs title: "Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models"; authors Brandon T. Willard, Rémi Louf.
items.supports: Regex- and grammar-guided generation can be recast as finite-state-machine transitions with a precomputed vocabulary index, which is the method behind the Outlines library.
items.relation_to_us: A foundational engine for the grammar side of our 2x2; we run no local engine. Outlines limits JSON whitespace by default (whitespace_pattern r"[ ]?"), and its documentation gives the reason that small models fall into infinite repetition when whitespace is unbounded: a direct contrast with XGrammar's unbounded default, and practitioner evidence that the runaway is known. That passage is from the Outlines docs, not from this paper.
items.notes: Metadata verified on arXiv. The Outlines whitespace default and its stated reason were confirmed through the Outlines JSON docs (via search) and independently by Li et al. (COLM 2025, Appendix C.9), which says JSON generation in Outlines "can output infinite whitespaces" and that Outlines therefore chose a single-space whitespace pattern. Cite the docs or Li et al. for the whitespace point, not this paper.

items.title: Grammar-Aligned Decoding
items.authors: Kanghee Park, Jiayu Wang, Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick, Nadia Polikarpova, Loris D'Antoni
items.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (NeurIPS 2024), Main Conference Track; arXiv 2405.21047
items.evidence: NeurIPS proceedings page: "Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (NeurIPS 2024) Main Conference Track"; arXiv comment: "Accepted to NeurIPS 2024".
items.supports: Grammar-constrained decoding distorts the model's distribution, so grammatical outputs are not sampled in proportion to the model's own probabilities, and ASAp corrects this toward the grammar-conditioned distribution.
items.relation_to_us: The peer-reviewed general mechanism behind our failure: masking and renormalising push mass onto continuations the model would not choose, such as whitespace once the token it wants is masked. We do not repair the decoder, which a router client cannot do; we remove the grammar from the long reading call and keep it only for the short judgement call.
items.notes: Title, authors and venue match. The evaluation domains (program synthesis, constituency parsing) come from repo notes and were not rechecked here.

items.title: Guiding LLMs The Right Way: Fast, Non-Invasive Constrained Generation
items.authors: Luca Beurer-Kellner, Marc Fischer, Martin Vechev
items.venue: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024), PMLR 235:3658-3673; arXiv 2403.06988
items.evidence: PMLR page: "Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235:3658-3673, 2024."
items.supports: Constrained decoding can significantly impair task accuracy when the LLM's subword vocabulary is not aligned with the constraint, and DOMINO enforces constraints in a subword-aligned way with virtually no overhead.
items.relation_to_us: A second mechanism for quality loss under grammars: a token boundary is not a grammar boundary, and at a JSON key position the legal tokens are only whitespace, a quote or a brace. Context for why grammar-constrained long JSON behaves differently from the same JSON described in the prompt; we did not test it as the cause of anything we saw.
items.notes: arXiv abstract: DOMINO achieves "virtually no overhead and in some cases even almost 2x speedup over unconstrained decoding", matching the candidate.

items.title: CRANE: Reasoning with constrained LLM generation
items.authors: Debangshu Banerjee, Tarun Suresh, Shubham Ugare, Sasa Misailovic, Gagandeep Singh
items.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267:2836-2857; arXiv 2502.09061
items.evidence: PMLR page: "Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267:2836-2857, 2025."
items.supports: Restricting output to a grammar that admits only final answers can reduce LLM reasoning, and alternating unconstrained reasoning with constrained answer spans (CRANE) recovers it, with up to 10 points of accuracy gain on symbolic reasoning benchmarks.
items.relation_to_us: The same idea as our reading+judgement split, done inside a single decode with an extended grammar: free-form content first, then enforced structure. Ours does it as two API calls, a reading call without a grammar (validated afterwards) and a grammar-constrained judgement over the checked claims, which is the only form available to a hosted-API client. Their tasks are short symbolic reasoning; ours is long extraction with quotations.
items.notes: Not previously verified in the repo; now verified on PMLR and arXiv (arXiv comment: "Accepted at ICML 2025"). The benchmark names GSM-symbolic and FOLIO come from the candidate and were not rechecked; the abstract says only 'challenging symbolic reasoning benchmarks'.

items.title: The Hidden Cost of Structured Generation in LLMs: Draft-Conditioned Constrained Decoding
items.authors: Avinash Reddy, Thayne T. Walker, James S. Ide, Amrit Singh Bedi
items.venue: ICML 2026 (main-conference poster, 8 Jul 2026, per icml.cc); arXiv 2603.03305 (v2 27 Jun 2026)
items.evidence: icml.cc: "ICML Poster The Hidden Cost of Structured Generation in LLMs: Draft-Conditioned Constrained Decoding"; arXiv abstract: "reduces the cumulative 'projection tax' induced by hard constraints".
items.supports: Constrained decoding can push generation toward locally valid but semantically wrong continuations when valid tokens have little probability, and decoding under the constraint after an unconstrained draft (DCCD) raises strict structured accuracy by up to 24 points (GSM8K, 1B model: 15.2% to 39.0%).
items.relation_to_us: The closest analogue of the 'design' axis of our 2x2: free generation first, then a constrained call. Their second pass re-emits the same answer under the constraint, while our judgement call is a different task (summary, gaps, ATT&CK) over claims the locator has already checked. Their outputs are short; our reading output runs to thousands of tokens. It supports keeping the grammar off the long free-content call.
items.notes: Author names differ by source: arXiv gives 'Thayne T. Walker' and 'James S. Ide'; the ICML virtual page gives 'Thayne Walker' and 'Jaime Ide'. Use the arXiv form until the PMLR page is out. No PMLR proceedings page (vol. 306 per repo notes) was found by search; cite as ICML 2026 with the arXiv ID and add PMLR volume and pages once published.

items.title: TruncProof: A Guardrail for LLM-based JSON Generation under Token-Length Constraints
items.authors: Yoshio Kato, Shuhei Tarashima
items.venue: arXiv 2605.13076 (v3 24 Jun 2026); arXiv comment states accepted at IJCNN 2026 (self-reported; no IEEE Xplore record found)
items.evidence: arXiv Comments: "Main paper (8 pages). Accepted at the International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN 2026)"; abstract: "leading to infinite generation or truncated outputs that cause a system malfunction."
items.supports: Grammar-constrained JSON generation cannot by itself enforce a maximum token count, which leads to infinite generation or truncated output; TruncProof uses LL(1) parser properties to keep JSON valid within a token limit.
items.relation_to_us: The closest treatment of our whitespace-runaway failure, but fixed inside the decoder with a tight budget on short JSON. Our budget is generous (about 40k tokens), the model is hosted behind a router, and the loops do not end. Our mitigation is on the application side: drop the grammar, validate after decoding, re-ask at most twice. A different method for the same failure, at a layer they control and we cannot.
items.notes: Title and authors match arXiv. peer_reviewed is set false only because the IJCNN acceptance is self-reported in the arXiv comment and no proceedings record was found (a search on 2026-10-03 returned none); change to true and cite IJCNN 2026 / IEEE WCCI proceedings once IEEE Xplore lists it. The baseline numbers (Outlines, SynCode, XGrammar at 1-36% syntax accuracy; Gemma2-2B, Llama2-7B) and the whitespace attribution come from repo notes and were not rechecked here.

items.title: Correctness-Guaranteed Code Generation via Constrained Decoding
items.authors: Lingxiao Li, Salar Rahili, Yiwei Zhao
items.evidence: arXiv Comments: "Published at COLM 2025"; PDF: "Nontermination is a well-known issue in constrained decoding; it is part of the more general issue of distribution distortion".
items.supports: Non-termination, where constrained decoding corners the model into endless repetition, is a known failure of constrained decoding, and its authors report that JSON-schema decoding in Outlines could emit infinite whitespace.
items.relation_to_us: Peer-reviewed support for treating non-termination under a grammar as a known failure rather than a quirk of one provider. It gives no rate for a deployed JSON application; our contribution is that measurement (runaway rate, failed cases, cost) plus the prompt-plus-validation alternative.
items.notes: Verified from the arXiv abs page and the PDF header ('Published as a conference paper at COLM 2025'). The PDF confirms that their own failures were runs that "did not terminate after the output token limit" (counted as failure above 1500 output tokens), and Appendix C.9 notes infinite whitespace in Outlines JSON generation and similar reports for ollama and OpenAI JSON mode. The COLM accepted-papers page was found by search but not opened.

items.title: Instructor (Python library: structured outputs for LLMs, Pydantic validation with retries)
items.authors: Jason Liu, Ivan Leo and contributors (567-labs)
items.venue: Open-source software (GitHub 567-labs/instructor, MIT license); not peer-reviewed
items.evidence: GitHub description: "structured outputs for llms"; README: "Failed validations are automatically retried with the error message".
items.supports: Instructor validates an LLM's reply against a Pydantic model and, with max_retries, sends a failed validation back to the model with the error message to ask again.
items.relation_to_us: Prior art for both of our components; we claim novelty for neither. The reading call is this validate-and-re-ask pattern, capped at two re-asks. Our locator extends Instructor's quote-in-source check with NFKC, ellipsis pieces, markup tolerance and the format-only tier. Unlike a retry loop, an unlocated quote is not re-asked: the claim stays 'not confirmed' and a near-match pointer is shown for a person to judge.
items.notes: Authors from PyPI (Author: Jason Liu, Ivan Leo; maintainer jxnl). The 2023 citation-verification example exists as the blog post 'Verifying LLM Citations with Pydantic' (python.useinstructor.com/blog/2023/11/18/validate-citations/) and the docs page 'exact_citations'; search snippets describe a substring check and a whitespace-normalised check, but the exact 'exact first, then normalised' order was not read on the page here.

items.title: TypeChat (library) / 'Introducing TypeChat' announcement post
items.authors: Anders Hejlsberg, Steve Lucco, Daniel Rosenwasser, Pierce Boggan, Umesh Madan, Mike Hopcroft, Gayathri Chandrasekaran (Microsoft)
items.venue: Open-source software (GitHub microsoft/TypeChat) and blog post 'Introducing TypeChat'; not peer-reviewed
items.evidence: Post: "we can validate the response against them using the TypeScript compiler itself!" and "the error feedback from the compiler can even be used to guide repairs."
items.supports: TypeChat describes the expected response as TypeScript types in the prompt, validates the JSON reply with the TypeScript compiler, and uses the compiler errors to ask the model for a repair.
items.relation_to_us: The same pattern as our reading call: the JSON shape is described in the prompt, nothing is enforced while decoding, the reply is validated in code, and a failed reply is asked again. A precedent for the 'validation after decoding' cell of our 2x2; we compare it with grammar-constrained decoding on long outputs rather than proposing it.
items.notes: Title, byline and date match the post ("Introducing TypeChat", July 20, 2023). The GitHub repo itself was not opened.

items.title: Guardrails (Guardrails AI: validation framework for LLM output with re-asking)
items.authors: Guardrails AI (guardrails-ai organisation)
items.venue: Open-source software (GitHub guardrails-ai/guardrails, Apache-2.0); not peer-reviewed
items.evidence: Docs page 'Validator OnFail Actions': "You can set `num_reasks` on the `guard()` call to determine how many times we retry."
items.supports: Guardrails runs validators over LLM output, each with an on-fail action (REASK, FIX, FILTER, REFRAIN, NOOP, EXCEPTION, FIX_REASK, CUSTOM), and num_reasks caps how often it asks the model again.
items.relation_to_us: Prior art for validation after decoding with a bounded re-ask; our cap of two re-asks corresponds to num_reasks=2. Our quotation locator is a deterministic validator whose on-fail action is closest to NOOP plus a flag: the claim is kept but marked 'not confirmed' and shown with its nearest source passage. We neither FIX the quote nor re-ask for it, so a person, not the model, decides.
items.notes: On-fail action names and num_reasks confirmed on the docs page; release dates, author field and license from PyPI. The GitHub repo itself was not opened.

themes.theme: Application domain: information extraction from police/crime narratives and cyber-incident text, LLMs used instead of trained NER/IE, LLM-written reports in digital forensics and incident response, and multi-stage extract-then-reason LLM pipelines for grounded analysis

items.title: CASIE: Extracting Cybersecurity Event Information from Text
items.authors: Taneeya Satyapanich, Francis Ferraro, Tim Finin
items.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 34(05) (AAAI-20 Technical Tracks 5), pp. 8749-8757
items.evidence: ojs.aaai.org landing page: "CASIE: Extracting Cybersecurity Event Information from Text" ... "Vol. 34 No. 05: AAAI-20 Technical Tracks 5", pp. 8749-8757, published April 3, 2020.
items.supports: There is a human-annotated corpus of English cyber-incident news with event types, triggers and arguments (CASIE), and its gold arguments can serve as an independent reference for which case facts an analysis quotes.
items.relation_to_us: Same kind of text, different task. CASIE is our evaluation corpus: its gold event arguments are what citation coverage is measured against. CASIE's own system is a trained event extractor that fills a fixed schema; CyberCase writes free-form claims with quotations, so CASIE measures whether gold facts are quoted, not argument F1.
items.notes: All fields match the AAAI OJS landing page. No corrections.

items.title: Crime data mining: a general framework and some examples
items.authors: Hsinchun Chen, Wingyan Chung, Jennifer J. Xu, Gang Wang, Yi Qin, Michael Chau (Crossref: H. Chen, W. Chung, J.J. Xu, G. Wang, Y. Qin, M. Chau)
items.venue: Computer (IEEE Computer Society) 37(4), pp. 50-56, April 2004 (research feature)
items.evidence: Author PDF, p. 55: "The modified extractor performed well in identifying person names (74.1 percent) and narcotic drugs (85.4 percent) from the test data set, but not as well for addresses (59.6 percent) and personal properties (46.8 percent)."
items.supports: Getting structure out of police narratives has long been a goal: COPLINK adapted a rule-plus-neural-network entity extractor to 36 noisy Phoenix narcotics reports, with good results for person names and drugs but weak results for addresses and personal properties.
items.relation_to_us: Precedent for the domain goal of structuring police narratives. Extracted entities are spans of the text, so traceable by construction, but each entity type needs labels, rules or training, and no summary or judgement is written. CyberCase replaces the trained extractor with an LLM reading and restores traceability with the deterministic quote locator.
items.notes: Title, authors, volume, issue, pages and year match Crossref; passage read in the author PDF (pweb.fbe.hku.hk/~mchau/papers/CrimeDataMiningFramework.pdf). The percentages quoted are the first set (precision implied: the next sentence gives 'Recalls for the same categories were 73.4, 77.9, 51.4, and 47.8 percent'). Source inconsistency: the five entity types are listed as person names, addresses, vehicles, narcotic names and physical characteristics, yet results are reported for 'personal properties'. Vehicles were not scored (only four mentions). Peer review: research features in IEEE Computer are refereed, but the review status was not read on a landing page. Chau, Xu and Chen 2002 (dg.o) page conflict stays open: Chen et al. 2004 ref. 5 reads 'pp. 271-275'; a search index summary gives pp. 1-5 (probably the ACM DL per-paper numbering); DBLP and Semantic Scholar were blocked (403/429), so resolve before citing the 2002 paper.

items.title: Entity Extraction of Key Elements in 110 Police Reports Based on Large Language Models
items.authors: Xintao Xing, Peng Chen
items.evidence: Crossref abstract: "employing large language models specific to the public security domain for entity extraction. Several lightweight (6/7b) open-source large language models were tested as base models."
items.supports: LLMs have already been applied in place of traditional NER to extract key elements from Chinese police reports, with LoRA fine-tuning (+10-50% F1), prompt engineering (about +3%) and ChatGPT-based augmentation (about +4% more), beating a fine-tuned UIE model by about 5% per element.
items.relation_to_us: Same goal, different method. The clearest police-report case of an LLM used in place of a trained NER/IE model, but it still fine-tunes and scores entity F1 against labels. CyberCase does not fine-tune and has no entity schema; it checks each claim's quotation against the source instead.
items.notes: Title, authors, volume, issue, article number and year match Crossref; the abstract was read verbatim from the Crossref record (MDPI page returned 403). Refinement of what_it_does: the base models are lightweight 6/7B open-source LLMs (Baichuan best), described as 'specific to the public security domain'; the test data are 2019 police reports from one city; the UIE comparison also reports a 42% F1 gain on the 'organization' element; ChatGPT is also used to align extracted entities.

items.title: Using Instruction-Tuned Large Language Models to Identify Indicators of Vulnerability in Police Incident Narratives
items.authors: Sam Relins, Daniel Birks, Charlie Lloyd
items.venue: Journal of Quantitative Criminology 41(4), pp. 647-684, December 2025 (Springer)
items.evidence: arXiv 2412.11878 abstract: "IT-LLMs are highly effective at screening narratives where no vulnerabilities are present, potentially vastly reducing the requirement for human coding." RePEc: "Journal of Quantitative Criminology, Springer, vol. 41(4), pages 647-684, December 2025".
items.supports: Instruction-tuned LLMs have been compared with human coders on Boston Police narratives for four vulnerability indicators, with label variability measured over repeated prompts and counterfactual sex/race bias tested.
items.relation_to_us: Precedent for using LLMs on police narratives in place of human coding and for measuring variability across repeated prompts. Their task is document-level classification against human coders, with no quotation grounding; CyberCase writes claims with verbatim quotations and checks traceability, not label agreement.
items.notes: Title, authors, venue, volume, issue, pages and year match Crossref and RePEc. The 'highly effective at screening' wording is from the arXiv preprint abstract; the published abstract instead says 'LLMs demonstrate high agreement with human coders in identifying narratives without vulnerabilities', so quote the published wording when citing the journal version. Models (Llama 8B and 70B, GPT-4o) are not in either abstract but were confirmed in the open-access published PDF (eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/228974). The published abstract says 'sex and race', not 'gender'.

items.title: TextEE: Benchmark, Reevaluation, Reflections, and Future Challenges in Event Extraction
items.authors: Kuan-Hao Huang, I-Hung Hsu, Tanmay Parekh, Zhiyu Xie, Zixuan Zhang, Prem Natarajan, Kai-Wei Chang, Nanyun Peng, Heng Ji
items.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2024, pp. 12804-12825 (doi:10.18653/v1/2024.findings-acl.760)
items.evidence: ACL Anthology abstract: "We also evaluate five varied large language models on our TextEE benchmark and demonstrate how they struggle to achieve satisfactory performance."
items.supports: Under a standardized protocol over 16 datasets (CASIE among them) and 14 methods, prompted LLMs still trail trained event extractors on gold event-argument scores.
items.relation_to_us: Caution for our framing: CyberCase should not claim its LLM reading is a better extractor than trained systems. It uses CASIE's gold for citation coverage and traceable-claim rate, not argument F1. TextEE's protocol is also the one AEC uses on CASIE.
items.notes: All metadata match the ACL Anthology page. The abstract confirms '16 datasets spanning eight diverse domains' and '14 recent methodologies'. CASIE confirmed in the official README (github.com/ej0cl6/TextEE): 'CASIE | E2E, ED, EAE'.

items.title: Decompose, Enrich, and Extract! Schema-aware Event Extraction using LLMs
items.authors: Fatemeh Shiri, Farhad Moghimifar, Reza Haffari, Yuan-Fang Li, Van Nguyen, John Yoo (published order per Crossref; arXiv 2406.01045 lists Fatemeh Shiri, Van Nguyen, Farhad Moghimifar, John Yoo, Gholamreza Haffari, Yuan-Fang Li)
items.venue: 2024 27th International Conference on Information Fusion (FUSION), pp. 1-8
items.evidence: arXiv 2406.01045 abstract: "introducing a new method to address hallucination by decomposing the task into Event Detection and Event Argument Extraction." Crossref container: "2024 27th International Conference on Information Fusion (FUSION)", pp. 1-8.
items.supports: Splitting LLM event extraction into detection and then argument extraction, each with schema-aware retrieved examples, has been proposed to reduce hallucination and outperforms direct baselines on event-extraction benchmarks.
items.relation_to_us: Precedent for the 'one call vs staged calls' arm of our 2x2. Their decomposition helps extraction under gold annotations; our split is reading (claims with quotations) then judgement over checked claims only, crossed with grammar vs validation-after-decoding, which they do not study.
items.notes: Title, venue, pages and year match Crossref. Author order confirmed to differ between Crossref and arXiv; Crossref spells the third author 'Reza Haffari', arXiv 'Gholamreza Haffari'. Cite the published (Crossref) order.

items.title: Extracting Events Like Code: A Multi-Agent Programming Framework for Zero-Shot Event Extraction
items.authors: Quanjiang Guo, Sijie Wang, Jinchuan Zhang, Ben Zhang, Zhao Kang, Ling Tian, Ke Yan
items.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 40(37), pp. 30880-30887 (arXiv 2511.13118 is the preprint, 'accepted by AAAI 2026 (Oral)')
items.evidence: arXiv 2511.13118 (HTML): "we follow the TextEE evaluation protocol ... For CASIE, due to its smaller size, we sample 50 test instances." Crossref: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 40(37), 30880-30887.
items.supports: A multi-agent LLM pipeline (retrieval, planning, coding, verification) that renders event schemas as executable classes for deterministic validation has been evaluated zero-shot on five domains including CASIE under the TextEE protocol.
items.relation_to_us: Closest multi-stage LLM pipeline evaluated on CASIE, and it also pairs LLM output with a deterministic check. Their check validates schema conformance; ours locates each quotation in the source. AEC iterates until output is valid, whereas CyberCase re-asks at most twice and otherwise leaves the claim 'not confirmed'.
items.notes: Metadata match Crossref and the arXiv abs page. The five datasets (FewEvent, ACE 2005, GENIA, SPEED, CASIE), the TextEE protocol and the 50 CASIE test instances were confirmed in the arXiv HTML full text; the abstract itself names only 'five diverse domains'.

items.title: ChatGPT, Llama, can you write my report? An experiment on assisted digital forensics reports written using (local) large language models

items.venue: Forensic Science International: Digital Investigation 48, article 301683 (DFRWS EU 2024)

ScienceDirect and the dfrws.org PDF returned 403, so the abstract was read on the arXiv preprint (2312.14607, comment 'Accepted for publication at the Digital Forensics Research Conference (DFRWS EU) 2024'), not the open-access publisher PDF as the candidate states. Cite the journal DOI.

items.title: Structured Report Generation using Local LLMs for Chat-Based Digital Forensics
items.authors: Ying Dehing, Hans Henseler, Timo Meconi, Marcel Worring, Harm van Beek
items.venue: Proceedings of the Digital Forensics Doctoral Symposium (DFDS 2026, Linköping, Sweden), ACM, pp. 1-11
items.evidence: Crossref: "Structured Report Generation using Local LLMs for Chat-Based Digital Forensics"; container "Proceedings of the Digital Forensics Doctoral Symposium"; publisher ACM; pages 1-11; event "DFDS 2026: Digital Forensics Doctoral Symposium" (Linköping, Sweden).

items.authors: Diana Kramer, Lambert Rosique, Ajay Narotam, Elie Bursztein, Patrick Gage Kelley, Kurt Thomas, Allison Woodruff
items.venue: Twenty-First Symposium on Usable Privacy and Security (SOUPS 2025), Seattle, WA, August 2025, USENIX, pp. 133-148
items.evidence: USENIX abstract: "producing summaries that omit critical details in 35% of cases and/or inject factual inaccuracies in 42% of cases."
items.supports: In a study with 18 security analysts and 50 real incidents, autonomous LLM incident summaries omitted critical details in 35% of cases and/or injected factual inaccuracies in 42%, while collaborative use reduced analyst effort.
items.relation_to_us: Same goal of LLM analysis of incident narratives, and the motivating evidence that autonomous LLM summaries omit facts and add inaccuracies. Their remedy is human editing with no source-level citation; CyberCase's is per-claim verbatim quotations located in the source, with unlocated quotes left 'not confirmed' and shown with a near-match pointer.
items.notes: Title, authors, venue and pages match the USENIX page (ISBN 978-1-939133-51-9). The abstract names no model: 'Gemini 1.5 Flash' and the counts 73/211 and 89/211 come from the repo's full-text notes, not the landing page. The abstract says collaborative use reduces effort 'while improving the readability and consistency of summaries'; 'analysts preferred the AI-assisted summaries' is also from the repo notes, not the abstract.

items.title: Forensic Schema for Psychological Manipulation in Cyber Fraud: LLM-Driven Victim Reports Analysis
items.authors: Zikai Alex Wen, Corrazon Ogot, Juan Li, Yan Bai
items.venue: arXiv:2607.07751 (preprint, submitted 8 Jul 2026); arXiv comment: accepted by PST 2026 (23rd International Conference on Privacy, Security and Trust); proceedings not yet seen
items.evidence: arXiv abstract: "victim narratives varied widely in the actionable detail supporting each Yes answer, and blockchain-specific identifiers were nearly absent." Comments: "Accepted by the 23rd International Conference on Privacy, Security and Trust (PST 2026)".
items.supports: LLM annotation of 10,994 cyber-fraud victim reports with a 35-question forensic schema matched human agreement (kappa 0.69 vs 0.68 between annotators), but a rationale audit found narratives varied widely in actionable detail, pointing to schema-informed follow-up questions at intake.
items.relation_to_us: Closest application: LLM analysis of cybercrime victim narratives with rationales and detail gaps; it ends where CyberCase's gap list and follow-up begin. CyberCase adds what they leave open: each quotation is located in the source deterministically before any judgement uses the claim. Cite as a preprint until the PST proceedings appear.
items.notes: Title, authors and comment match the arXiv abs page. Correction to the candidate's quotation: the abstract reads 'varied widely in the actionable detail supporting each Yes answer', not 'in actionable detail supporting answers'. The count is 10,994 reports (the candidate's 'about 11,000' is fine as a paraphrase); the schema has four categories, 35 questions and 11 manipulation indicators; validation was against two human annotators.
